2. Visual acuity measurement #59

  • Optotype - tables with rows of letters/numbers, where the dimensions decrease from top to bottom.
  • Each row should be viewed from a specified distance (noted on each row).
  • The table is uniformly illuminated, and the patient stands at a certain distance.
  • Visual acuity is expressed as a fraction: the distance from which a row is read over the distance from which the row should be seen.
  • Normal visual acuity is represented by a fraction of 1 (e.g., 10/10, 20/20).
  • If visual acuity improves with a pinhole occluder, it may indicate a refractive error

2. Visual Field Examination through Confrontation Method. Detection of Bitemporal and Homonymous Hemianopsia #62

  • A. Both eyes open. Question: "Look at my nose; is there any part of my face missing?" Detects central scotomas, hemianopsia.
  • B. Each eye separately. Counting fingers in the quadrants → hemianopsias, quadrantanopsias. Comparing the right visual field with the left visual field ("Which finger is seen more clearly?") → less dense hemianopsias.
  • C. Each eye separately. Move the indicator from the periphery toward the center: "Specify when the indicator appears" → quadrantanopsias, altitudinal defects, paracentral scotomas.
  • The patient and the examiner stand at the same level, at a distance of 1 meter.
  • The patient covers one eye on the same side with their hand. The confrontation of the visual fields by the examiner is compared to those of the patient.
  • The indicator moves slowly, at an equal distance between the two."

Hemianopsias #63

  • Bitemporal - chiasmal lesion
  • Homonymous right - lesion in the left hemisphere
  • Homonymous left - lesion in the right hemisphere
  • Normal result: the patient counts fingers in all quadrants of both eyes. Bitemporal hemianopsia: the patient cannot count fingers in the temporal quadrants of each eye. Homonymous hemianopsia: the patient cannot count fingers in the temporal quadrants of one eye and the nasal quadrants of the other eye.

3. Evaluation of colour perception #64

  • The human eye is capable of perceiving the fundamental colours red, green, and blue thanks to three specific types of retinal cells called cones. Dichromacy is the term used when one type of receptor is missing. More specifically, it is referred to as:
  • Protanopia if red is not perceived
  • Deuteranopia if green is not perceived
  • Tritanopia if blue is not perceived
  • Anomalous trichromacy is used when one of the three types of receptors is deficient. The deficiency can vary from very mild to very severe, with the impairment being close to that of a dichromat. More specifically, it is referred to as:
  • Protanomaly if the perception of red is altered
  • Deuteranomaly if the perception of green is altered
  • Tritanomaly if the perception of blue is altered

4. Test with a pinhole. Subjective examination of ocular refraction. #71

  • pinhole—a solid disc with a central hole—to improve focusing by narrowing the beam of light. The objective is to detect refractive errors.
  • The process is as follows:
  • Measure visual acuity without a pinhole.
  • Measure visual acuity with a pinhole.
  • Interpretation: If visual acuity improves with a pinhole, it indicates a refractive error. This improvement occurs because the pinhole reduces the effects of certain refractive errors, such as myopia (nearsightedness) or astigmatism, by allowing only central rays of light to enter the eye. If there is an improvement, it suggests that the refractive error might be contributing to the visual impairment.

Slide 72 #72

Slide 74 #74

  • Visual acuity (VA) of 1 indicates either an emmetrope or a hypermetrope (hyperopic individual).
  • Place a +0.5 D lens in front of the eye:
  • If the patient sees less clearly, they are emmetropic.
  • If vision improves, it indicates hypermetropia.
  • To determine the value of hypermetropia, gradually increase the strength of "plus" lenses until the patient can read the last line.
  • If visual acuity is below 0.1, use a pinhole:
  • If vision improves, it suggests a refractive error.
  • If not, it may be an organic eye disease, and a lens of +/- 0.5 D is placed.
  • For hypermetropes, increase the "plus" until they can see the last line.
  • For myopes, increase the value until the lowest power with which they can see the last line.
  • If there's no improvement with either "+" or "-", it indicates astigmatism.

  • A. "Concomitant strabismus": This is a type of strabismus in which the deviation of the eyes remains constant regardless of the direction of gaze.

Slide 78 #78

  • B. "Incomitant strabismus" or "paralytic strabismus": Has a magnitude that varies when the person moves their gaze up, down, or to the sides. The eyes appear straight when looking to the right (up) and straight ahead (in the middle), but misalignment is evident when looking to the left (down), indicating paralysis of the left lateral rectus muscle or restriction of the left medial rectus muscle. These eye positions would be observed in a paralysis of the left sixth cranial nerve.

Cover test #79

  • Cover test (manifest strabismus) involves the following steps:
  • The patient is asked to focus their gaze on a target (toy).
  • Cover the eye that appears to be the fixating eye for a few seconds, while tracking the movement of the opposite eye (if it moves to take fixation).
  • Uncover the eye and observe whether it resumes fixation.

Cover-uncover test – latent strabismus #80

  • The steps are as follows:
  • The patient is asked to focus their gaze on a target (toy).
  • One eye is covered, and then quickly, the other eye is covered.
  • This process is repeated several times.
  • Observe if the eye moves upon uncovering.

8. Fluorescein coloration #109

  • Objective: Detection of corneal de-epithelialization/ulcerations
  • Procedure: Preparation: The patient is typically positioned behind a slit lamp. A fluorescein solution, often in the form of drops or an impregnated strip, is used.
  • Administration of Fluorescein: The doctor instills a few drops of fluorescein solution into the lower conjunctival fornix of the eye. The
  • patient may experience slight irritation or a temporary burning sensation. Observation under a Slit Lamp: After administering fluorescein, the doctor observes the eye using a slit lamp equipped with blue light.
  • Fluorescein reacts to blue light, emitting a fluorescent green colour when in contact with damaged cells or areas of the cornea where the outer protective layer is altered.
  • Evaluation of Ocular Surface: The doctor assesses the distribution and intensity of fluorescence to detect abnormalities such as corneal abrasions, ulcers, dryness, or other ocular surface issues.
  • This process can aid in diagnosing and monitoring corneal conditions.

Interpretation: #110

  • Positive: The cornea retains fluorescein (green) – indicating the presence of corneal epithelium damage.
  • Negative: The cornea does not absorb fluorescein – indicating the integrity of the epithelium. This is often performed to assess corneal health, especially to detect issues such as corneal epithelium damage or ulcers. Fluorescein, once instilled in the eye, reacts with damaged areas of the cornea and emits green fluorescence under blue light, facilitating the visual detection of these problems.

9. Detection of abnormal pupil: color, shape, contour, location, and diameter #112

  • a. Colour: The normal pupil is typically black.
  • b. Shape: The pupil should normally be round and symmetrical.
  • c. Contour: The contour of the pupil should be smooth.
  • d. Location: The pupil should be centered in the iris and symmetrical between the two eyes.
  • e. Diameter: The diameter of the pupil can vary based on lighting conditions. Anisocoria (difference in size between the two pupils) is possible.

Abnormal colour #113

  • White (leukocoria): Mature cataract, pupillary occlusion, retinoblastoma.
  • Yellowish: Endophthalmitis.
  • Reddish: Albinism (lack of melanin).

Abnormal shape and contour #114

  • Oval, vertically elongated: Glaucoma attack.
  • "Keyhole" shape: Iris coloboma.
  • Irregular contour: Posterior iris syndromes (sometimes clover-shaped).
  • Ruptures of the iris sphincter.

  • Acquired: Trauma, surgical interventions, iris inflammations

Diameter #116

  • Mydriasis (> 4 mm): Post-iris trauma, optic nerve trauma, glaucoma attack (partial mydriasis).

10. Pupillary reflexes #117

  • Direct Photomotor Reflex: This involves the pupillary constriction of the eye exposed to direct light. When bright light is directed toward the eye, the pupil constricts to reduce the amount of incoming light, known as direct pupillary constriction.
  • Consensual Photomotor Reflex: This involves the pupillary constriction of the eye not exposed to direct light but in response to light stimulating the other eye. The pupil of the eye opposite to the light source (non-illuminated eye) also undergoes constriction, known as consensual constriction.

11. The examination of the red pupillary reflex and the recognition of leukocoria #122

  • The doctor observes the color of the pupil using a slit lamp or a light source.
  • Light enters through the pupil and is reflected by the retina.
  • Decrease: Any condition that interferes with the passage of light (most frequently: cataracts).
  • With an ophthalmoscope, after the dilation of the patient's pupils.
  • Light is simultaneously projected into both eyes, allowing the observation of symmetry or asymmetry.
  • Leukocoria is characterized by a pupil that appears white instead of red when light is projected into the eye.

Leucocoria #123

  • 1. Retinoblastoma
  • Explanation: It is a malignant tumor of the retina, more common in children. Leukocoria, or a white reflection in the pupil, is one of the early signs of this disease.
  • 2. Congenital cataract
  • 3. Primary vitreous persistence: This is a congenital condition where there is a failure of regression of the primary vitreous, which can lead to visual impairment
  • 4. Coats’ disease: Coats' disease is a rare eye disorder characterized by abnormal development of blood vessels behind the retina. It can lead to retinal detachment and may present with leukocoria among other symptoms.

12. Digital tonometry #124

  • Objective: Evaluation of Intraocular Pressure (IOP)
  • It assesses only significant variations in IOP, providing qualitative indications rather than exact values. Digital tonometry can give a qualitative indication of intraocular pressure.
  • Procedure: The patient looks downward. Through the eyelids, both index fingers are applied alternately to the eyeball.
  • Interpretation:
  • HTIO: Acute glaucoma, congenital glaucoma ("glass globe").
  • hTIO: Damaged eyeball, post-traumatic (cessation of secretion), choroidal detachment, retinal detachment.
  • Simple and useful for emergency diagnosis: Acute glaucoma, damaged eyeball.
  • This procedure and interpretation are useful in emergency situations to quickly assess and diagnose conditions related to intraocular pressure, such as acute glaucoma or eye damage. The qualitative assessment helps in prompt decision-making for urgent medical care.

13. Using the Ophthalmoscope to Examine the Fundus (FO) and Identify a Normal Optic Disc #125

  • The ophthalmoscope is a crucial tool for examining the back of the eye (fundus) and identifying a normal optic disc. Here's a description of the process:
  • Procedure:
  • Preparation: Ensure the room is darkened to allow for optimal visualization.
  • Patient Positioning: Ask the patient to sit comfortably and focus on a distant point.
  • Ophthalmoscope Adjustment: Set the ophthalmoscope to the appropriate lens for your vision (if applicable) and adjust the light intensity.
  • Approach: Stand about an arm's length away from the patient. Begin with the right eye.
  • Examination of the Optic Disc:
  • Direct Ophthalmoscopy: Direct the ophthalmoscope light toward the patient's right eye.
  • Pupil Examination: Observe the red reflex, ensuring the pupil is dilated.
  • Alignment: Align the ophthalmoscope with the visual axis of the eye, and approach the patient at a 15-degree angle temporally.
  • Optic Disc Inspection: Focus on the optic disc, located on the nasal side of the retina. Look for the following characteristics of a normal optic disc:
  • Color: It should be pink to yellowish-pink.
  • Margins: Well-defined margins.
  • Cup-to-Disc Ratio: The cup (central depression) should not exceed one-third of the disc diameter.
  • Repeat the process for the left eye.
  • Interpretation:
  • A normal optic disc is characterized by its pinkish to yellowish-pink color, well-defined margins, and an appropriate cup-to-disc ratio.

13. Using the Ophthalmoscope to Examine the Fundus (FO) and Identify a Normal Optic Disc #126

  • A. Direct Ophthalmoscopy:
  • Direct ophthalmoscope image, magnified by approximately 15x. Pupillary dilation a few minutes before.
  • Red pupillary reflex. Focused on the patient's retina.
  • Conditions: Transparent media.
  • Refractive error in both eyes - similar.

Direct ophthalmoscopy #127

  • Observer: The observer uses an ophthalmoscope and looks directly into the patient's eye.
  • Observed Image: The observed image is oriented directly and is mirrored in relation to the patient's gaze direction. This means that the observer sees an upright image of the fundus.
  • Advantages: Direct vision offers better image resolution and detailed observation of ocular structures, especially the optic disc and macula.
  • Disadvantages: The patient's pupil must be dilated to allow adequate visualization, and it can be more challenging to observe peripheral areas of the fundus.
  • Indirect ophthalmoscopy
  • Observer: The observer uses a condensing lens (such as a Goldman lens) and observes the patient's eye through a small opening in the lens.
  • Observed Image: The observed image is inverted and is generally smaller than that observed with direct ophthalmoscopy.
  • Advantages: Indirect vision allows for easier observation of peripheral areas of the fundus. It can be used with undilated pupils.
  • Disadvantages: The image resolution may be slightly lower than that of direct ophthalmoscopy.

Diabetic macular oedema #135

  • The fluid from leaking blood vessels accumulates in the central area of the retina, known as the macula, causing swelling of this area (macular edema).

Retinal Vascular Changes in Arterial Hypertension: #136

  • Arteriolar Narrowing:
  • Description: Constriction or narrowing of retinal arterioles.
  • Explanation: Elevated blood pressure can lead to the thickening and narrowing of arterioles in the retina.
  • Arteriovenous Nicking:
  • Description: Compression of retinal venules at arteriovenous crossings.
  • Explanation: Increased pressure in the arteries can compress the veins at their crossings, causing characteristic nicking.

Hypertensive retinopathy #137

  • Flame-Shaped Hemorrhages:
  • Description: Hemorrhages with a flame-shaped appearance.
  • Explanation: Rupture of small blood vessels in the retina due to increased pressure can lead to flame-shaped hemorrhages.
  • Cotton-Wool Spots:
  • Description: Soft, fluffy white lesions.
  • Explanation: Micro-infarcts in the nerve fiber layer caused by impaired blood flow.
  • Hard Exudates:
  • Description: Yellowish deposits.
  • Explanation: Lipid or protein deposits in the retina due to leakage from damaged blood vessels.
  • Optic Disc Swelling (Papilledema):
  • Description: Swelling of the optic disc.
  • Explanation: Elevated blood pressure can affect the optic nerve head, leading to papilledema.

Hypertensive neuropathy #138

15. Using the Ophthalmoscope to Detect: Papilledema, Glaucomatous Cupping, and Optic Atrophy #139

  • Optic Disc Swelling:
  • Description: This swelling is usually visible as an elevation of the optic disc.
  • Explanation: Swelling of the optic disc can occur due to various conditions, such as papilledema, where increased intracranial pressure affects the optic nerve head.
  • Blurred Disc Margins:
  • Description: The edges of the optic disc may appear blurry due to fluid accumulation, giving a faded appearance to the boundary between the disc and the retina.
  • Explanation: Blurred disc margins can be a sign of optic disc edema, often associated with increased intracranial pressure or other optic nerve head abnormalities.
  • Loss of Blood Vessel Definition:
  • Description: Due to swelling, blood vessels passing through the optic disc may appear less distinct or may even be partially obscured.
  • Explanation: Optic disc swelling can affect the visibility of blood vessels, leading to a loss of definition.
  • Papillary Color:
  • Description: The color of the optic disc may seem paler than normal due to swelling and altered blood perfusion.
  • Explanation: Changes in optic disc color can be indicative of underlying conditions affecting blood flow and tissue perfusion, such as papilledema.

Enlargement of the Optic Cup in Glaucoma: In glaucoma, the cup enlarges, resulting in a larger and deeper central depression within the optic disc #140

Optic nerve atrophy #141

  • Optic atrophy is characterized by a pale appearance of the optic disc
  • Causes:
  • 1. Glaucoma: Increased intraocular pressure can lead to optic nerve damage.
  • 2. Ischemic Optic Neuropathy: Reduced blood flow to the optic nerve.
  • 3. Optic Neuritis: Inflammation of the optic nerve.
  • 4. Trauma: Physical injury to the optic nerve.
  • 5. Hereditary Conditions: Genetic factors can contribute to optic nerve atrophy.
